matched_title: Server-side handling for `tags` is missing

findings.title: Server-side handling for `tags` is missing
findings.rationale: The `tags` field is added to the server-side Zod schema, but no corresponding server logic (e.g., storage, retrieval, or pass-through) is included in this PR. Clients that send `tags` will have them silently dropped because the server does not persist or return them. This violates the contract expectation that the `Finding` object includes the `tags` field when provided. Existing callers that do not use `tags` are unaffected, but new callers relying on the field will experience silent data loss.

findings.title: React key uses tag value which may not be unique
findings.rationale: The client renders tags using `key={tag}`. If a finding has duplicate tags (e.g., `['flaky', 'flaky']`), React will see duplicate keys, which can cause rendering issues and warnings. While tags are expected to be unique per finding, the contract does not enforce uniqueness, so this is a potential bug.

matched_title: Server-side handling for `tags` field is absent

findings.title: Server-side handling for `tags` field is absent
findings.rationale: The contract now defines `tags: z.array(z.string()).max(5).nullish()`, but the diff includes no server-side changes to persist, validate, or return this field. The PR description explicitly states 'without adding a whole new taxonomy or a migration', implying no database column is added. If the server uses a relational schema with separate columns, saving a finding with `tags` will fail. If it uses a JSON column, the field may be accepted but never returned, making the client rendering dead code. Existing callers are unaffected because the field is optional, but new clients that send `tags` may encounter 500 errors or silent data loss.

findings.title: Tags array may contain duplicates, causing React key collisions
findings.rationale: The client renders tags using `key={tag}`, which assumes each tag string is unique within the array. The Zod schema does not enforce uniqueness, so duplicate tags would produce duplicate keys, triggering React warnings and potential rendering issues.

matched_title: Breaking change: POST /agents now returns 200 instead of 201

findings.title: Breaking change: POST /agents now returns 200 instead of 201
findings.rationale: The response status code for creating an agent was changed from 201 (Created) to 200 (OK). Any deployed caller that checks for 201 — e.g., to trigger post-creation logic, to distinguish creation from update, or in test assertions — will now receive 200 and may behave incorrectly. This is a contract break because the HTTP status is part of the API contract.

matched_title: Breaking change: create-agent response status code changed from 201 to 200

findings.title: Breaking change: create-agent response status code changed from 201 to 200
findings.rationale: The create-agent handler previously returned HTTP 201 (Created) and now returns 200 (OK). Any deployed client that checks for 201 — whether in the web client, e2e tests, CI runner, or external consumer — will break. The semantic difference matters: 201 signals resource creation, while 200 is a generic success. This is a contract change that requires coordinated client updates.

matched_title: Breaking change: agent creation status code changed from 201 to 200

findings.title: Breaking change: agent creation status code changed from 201 to 200
findings.rationale: The `POST /agents` handler previously returned HTTP 201 (Created) on success. This diff changes it to return 200 (OK). Any deployed caller that checks for `status === 201` to determine that a new resource was created will now see 200 and may behave incorrectly — for example, failing to navigate to the new agent's detail page, not showing a success toast, or treating the response as an update rather than a creation. This is a contract break with no migration path.

matched_title: Breaking change: create agent endpoint now returns 200 instead of 201

findings.title: Breaking change: create agent endpoint now returns 200 instead of 201
findings.rationale: The HTTP status code for a successful agent creation is changed from 201 (Created) to 200 (OK). Any deployed caller that checks for 201 to distinguish creation from update, or to trigger post-creation logic (e.g., navigation, cache invalidation), will break. The PR description acknowledges this is one of four changes and that it is a breaking change.

findings.title: Client calls non-existent server endpoint
findings.rationale: The new `downloadFindingsCsv` function fetches `/pulls/${prId}/findings.csv`, but no server route for this path is present in the diff. Deploying this client code will cause all CSV export attempts to fail with a 404 error, breaking the feature for every user.

findings.title: CSV export request lacks authentication
findings.rationale: The `downloadFindingsCsv` function uses a plain `fetch` call without including credentials or authorization headers. The existing `apiFetch` function (used by all other API calls) likely attaches authentication tokens. Without them, the request will be rejected as unauthorized (401/403), breaking the export for all authenticated users.

findings.title: Server endpoint for CSV export is not implemented
findings.rationale: The new `downloadFindingsCsv` function fetches from `/pulls/:prId/findings.csv`, but no corresponding server route is defined in this PR. A deployed client that clicks the export button will receive a 404 error, breaking the feature entirely. This is a contract violation: the client expects an endpoint that does not exist.

findings.title: CSV export fetch does not include authentication headers
findings.rationale: The existing `apiFetch` wrapper (used by `api.get`, etc.) likely attaches authentication tokens (e.g., `Authorization: Bearer ...`). The new `downloadFindingsCsv` function uses a bare `fetch` with only `API_BASE`, omitting any auth. If the CSV endpoint requires authentication, all requests will fail with 401/403. This breaks the feature for authenticated users.

findings.title: Button onClick does not catch fetch errors
findings.rationale: The async `onClick` handler calls `downloadFindingsCsv` without a try-catch. If the fetch fails (network error, 404, 500), the promise rejection will be unhandled, causing a console error and no user feedback. This degrades user experience and can mask failures.

matched_title: Client-side shared contract not updated for new verdict

findings.title: Client-side shared contract not updated for new verdict
findings.rationale: The `Verdict` enum is defined in a shared contract that exists in two copies (server and client). This diff only updates the server copy to include `needs_discussion`. Any client that validates incoming responses against its own copy of the schema will reject the new value, causing a 422 or parse failure. The PR description explicitly states both copies must be changed together, but the client copy is not included in this diff.

matched_title: Client copy of shared contract not updated

findings.title: Client copy of shared contract not updated

findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/findings/dismiss-suggestions route calls getContext(container, req) and then service.dismissAllSuggestions(workspaceId, req.params.id) with no authorization check. The route also returns 204 with no body, so the caller gets no signal that the operation was rejected or succeeded, but the mutation happens server-side regardless. This is a real, exploitable defect: any authenticated user can silently modify findings on any PR in the system by guessing or enumerating PR ids.
